items.title: Which Masses are short.
items.body: An empty place stays coral until someone is in it. You see the holes in the month before the month arrives.

items.title: Who is owed a turn.
items.body: The same three people always say yes, so the same three people always serve. Here the list starts with whoever has served least.

items.title: Who quietly stopped coming.
items.body: A server who has not answered in three months does not look like a problem in a spreadsheet. In here, he does.

items.title: Nobody in two places at once.
items.body: Someone already in that Mass is not offered to you at all. Someone serving elsewhere that day, including at the novena running beside it, is flagged before you put their name down.

advantages.title: Four things a spreadsheet was never going to tell you.

assemblyPreview.caption: Example. Your own names and numbers appear here.

counters.body: While people are still answering, you see three numbers: how many have replied, how many have not, and how many Masses do not yet have enough servers.
counters.caption: Example from one month. Your own numbers appear here.
counters.followUp: Tap the last one and you get the list. Saturday, 7 p.m., the chapel: three servers needed, one available. So you write to the eight people who are missing instead of to all fifty-four, and you do it on Tuesday instead of on Saturday night.
counters.title: What the form never told you

items.q: Does anyone have to download anything?
items.a: No. Everything happens in the phone's browser, through the link you send to the group.

items.q: What about a server who has no smartphone?
items.a: Put them in yourself. When you are assembling, the list shows everybody, not only the people who answered.

items.q: We have more than one chapel. Does that work?
items.a: Yes. Chapels are part of your weekly pattern, and every Mass carries its own.

items.q: Can two of us coordinate together?
items.a: Yes. Invite the other coordinator and you work on the same schedules.

items.q: Our novena begins next week. Can I use it only for that?
items.a: Yes. A novena can have its own schedule, its own link and its own closing date, with no monthly schedule at all.

items.q: I was already invited to a parish. Can I still open my own?
items.a: An account belongs to one parish. If you were invited to one and need another, ask whoever administers the system.

final.body: Create your account, name your parish, and enter the Mass times of a normal week. You can have the link in the parish group the same evening.
final.passItOn: If this is useful, send this page to the coordinator at the parish next door. That is how it got to you.
final.reassurance: You do not have to move the whole ministry at once. Try it for one month and see how many people answer.
final.title: Start with one month.

footer.line: Altar Roster. For parish altar server ministries, under the patronage of Saint Tarcisius.

hero.headline: Send one link to the group. Your altar servers answer from their phones.
hero.serverAside: Are you an altar server who was sent a link? You don't need an account here. Open the link your coordinator sent you: it goes straight to your Masses.
hero.subheadline: Scheduling for parish altar server ministries. Set your weekly Mass times once, open the month, and send a single link to the parish group. Your servers mark the Masses they can serve. No account, no password, nothing to install.
hero.support: Your chapels and the Mass times of a normal week are entered once. Every month after that is generated from them.

noAccount.body: No sign-up, no password, nothing to install, nothing to download. They open the link, find their name, tap their Masses, and put the phone away. It works on an old phone and on a weak connection.
noAccount.claim: Anyone who wants an account later, so that only they can answer for their own name, can claim it. Nobody has to.
noAccount.privacy: The links you send carry names and Mass times, and nothing else: no member list, no telephone numbers, no e-mail addresses. Your parish sees only your parish.
noAccount.title: Your servers never create an account

novena.body: Nine evenings, places numbered one to six, and the servers claim them directly, exactly like the numbered list someone types into the group every year, except a place cannot be claimed twice.
novena.scope: A novena can live inside the month's schedule or stand on its own, with its own link and its own closing date. If someone is already serving at the same hour on the parish schedule, you are told before you publish.
novena.title: Novenas, the way your group already does them

recognition.closing: None of that is the ministry. It is the part standing between you and the ministry.
items: You build the form again, because last month's dates are wrong.
Twenty-two people answer. There are fifty-four names on your list, and the form does not tell you which thirty-two are missing.
You copy the answers into the spreadsheet and sort them by hand, trying to remember who served last Sunday and who has not served since Easter.
You take a screenshot of the table and send the picture to the group. Somebody asks which Mass is theirs.
Then, on Saturday night: “I'm so sorry, I can't serve tomorrow.” It sinks under two hundred other messages, and you find out at the sacristy door on Sunday morning.
recognition.title: You already know this part.

stats.body: At the end of the month you can see it plainly: the three who served every single week, the ones who have served once since Easter, and the ones who have not answered a form in two months.
stats.closing: It is not a ranking. It is how you notice the boy who quietly stopped coming, before a whole season has gone by.
stats.title: Who serves most. Who serves least. Who stopped coming.

items.title: Set it up once.
items.body: Your chapels, the Mass times of a normal week, and how many servers each Mass needs. You will not type a date again.

items.title: Open the month.
items.body: Every Mass appears, generated from that normal week. You adjust what is different this time: a feast, a funeral, the week the church is closed.

items.title: Send one link to the group.
items.body: Your servers open it, find their name, and filter to Sundays and mornings, and one tap marks all twelve dates at once. Then they are finished.

items.title: Build the schedule, slot by slot.
items.body: For each place you see who is available, who has served fewest times this month, and who is already serving somewhere else that day. You choose every name. The app never assigns anyone on its own.

items.title: Publish.
items.body: A read-only link goes back to the group: the finished schedule, on a phone, always current. No more screenshots that go out of date the moment something changes.

swap.body: It happens, and it is not a failure. The server opens their own Mass and asks for a replacement. That becomes a link you send to the group. The first person who taps it takes the place, the schedule updates itself, and the published link is already correct.
swap.closing: No message repeated three times, nobody waiting for an answer, and never two people showing up for the same slot.
swap.title: “I can't make it on Sunday.”

tarcisius.closing: That is all this is for.
tarcisius.figureAlt: Saint Tarcisius, holding the Eucharist against his chest
tarcisius.story: Rome, the third century. Tradition remembers a boy of about twelve who was trusted to carry the Eucharist across the city to Christians held in prison. He was stopped on the road and ordered to hand it over. He refused, and was killed still holding it. He was buried in the catacomb of Saint Callixtus, and the Church gave him to altar servers and to first communicants as their patron.
tarcisius.title: Under the patronage of Saint Tarcisius
tarcisius.today: Nothing of the sort is asked of the children in your sacristy. Only that they serve, and that somebody keeps track of who, carefully, and without anyone being forgotten.
